chunks.summary: Digital systems trace back to two-state signaling like telegraph Morse code; a timing diagram shows which of the two states (1/0) a signal is in over time.
chunks.text: A large part of the worldwide telecommunications system falls into the category of 'digital systems', which began as simple two-state signaling schemes. The classic example is the telegraph: a battery, a code key (a normally-open momentary switch), a wire, and an electromagnetic 'clacker' let an operator send only two distinct symbols -- short and long electrical pulses, i.e., the dots and dashes of Morse code. This is a digital representation of information because the electrical signal is always either fully on or fully off; modern digital systems are the direct descendant of this idea, using electrical signals to represent binary 1s and 0s. A timing diagram is the standard tool for visualizing this: it plots which state (1 or 0, HIGH or LOW) a signal is in at every point in time, and marks exactly when transitions between states occur. Test instruments such as oscilloscopes and logic analyzers are used to capture real timing diagrams so an engineer can compare actual circuit behavior against the expected/designed behavior.

chunks.summary: Analog representation varies continuously and proportionally (e.g., a microphone's voltage, a speedometer, a mercury thermometer); digital representation varies only in discrete steps (e.g., a digital clock's minute display).
chunks.text: Physical quantities that must be manipulated arithmetically can be represented either in analog or digital form. Analog representation is a continuously variable, proportional indicator: examples include a microphone converting sound pressure into a continuously varying voltage (a device pioneered by Alexander Graham Bell in 1875 to convert voice into an electrical signal, transmit it, and convert it back to sound), an automobile speedometer needle moving smoothly with speed, and a mercury thermometer whose column height varies continuously with temperature. Digital representation instead varies in discrete (separate) steps: a digital clock's displayed time jumps in one-minute increments rather than flowing smoothly, and a digital thermometer's displayed value changes only when the temperature shifts by at least one whole degree, never showing fractional in-between states.

chunks.topic: Digital and Analog Systems: Definitions, Advantages, and Limits
chunks.summary: A digital system manipulates discrete-valued information while an analog system manipulates continuously-valued quantities; digital's advantages (easier design, storage, accuracy, programmability, noise immunity, IC fabrication) are why the industry shifted to digital, despite the real world itself being analog and requiring conversion.
chunks.text: A digital system is a combination of devices designed to manipulate logical information or physical quantities that are represented only in digital form, i.e., quantities that can take on only discrete values. An analog system, by contrast, manipulates physical quantities represented in analog form, where quantities vary over a continuous range. Chief reasons the industry has shifted toward digital technology: (1) digital systems are generally easier to design, since exact voltage values do not matter -- only the range (HIGH or LOW) the signal falls into; (2) information storage is easy, e.g., in latches and memory chips, for as long as needed; (3) accuracy and precision are easier to maintain throughout a system, because digital signals are far less sensitive to component drift; (4) operations can be programmed, giving digital systems flexibility that pure analog hardware lacks; (5) digital circuits are less affected by electrical noise, since small voltage fluctuations don't change whether a signal is interpreted as a logic 1 or 0; and (6) more digital circuitry can be fabricated on IC chips than equivalent analog circuitry, driving down cost and size. Real-world examples of mixed digital/analog systems include: telephone party-lines, where the ringing/signaling was digital (encoded by crank pattern) but voice was purely analog; rotary-dial phones, which sent decimal digits as a series of pulses (digital) while touch-tone phones send digital switching information using analog tone signals; the modern cell phone, which has both digital and analog components; and a temperature-regulation system that uses an analog-to-digital converter (ADC) to bridge the analog physical world and digital control logic. There are limits to digital techniques: because the physical world itself is analog, using digital methods to control or measure it requires a time-consuming conversion pipeline: (1) convert the physical variable into an analog electrical signal (e.g., via a sensor/transducer), (2) convert that analog signal into digital form (via an ADC), (3) process/operate on the digital information, and (4) convert the digital output back into real-world analog form (via a digital-to-analog converter, DAC) to actually drive an actuator, speaker, display, etc.

chunks.topic: Digital Number Systems: Decimal and Binary Counting
chunks.summary: Understanding digital systems requires the decimal (base 10, 10 symbols), binary (base 2, 2 symbols), octal (base 8), and hexadecimal (base 16) numbering systems; a 4-bit binary counter cycles through 0000-1111 representing decimal 0-15.
chunks.text: Understanding digital systems requires understanding four numbering systems: decimal (base 10, symbols 0-9), hexadecimal (base 16, 16 symbols), octal (base 8, 8 symbols), and binary (base 2, symbols 0 and 1). In the decimal system, each symbol is called a digit (from the Latin for finger); the position of a digit gives it a positional value equal to the digit multiplied by a power of 10, with the most-significant digit (MSD) at the left and least-significant digit (LSD) at the right -- e.g., counting proceeds 0,1,2,...,19,20,21,...,99,100,101,...,999,1000. The binary system uses only 2 symbols (0, 1) and is naturally suited to electronic circuit design because it requires distinguishing only two voltage levels; each bit's positional value is a power of 2. A 4-bit binary counting table illustrates the mapping to decimal: weights are 2^3=8, 2^2=4, 2^1=2, 2^0=1 (the rightmost bit, 2^0, is the least-significant bit, LSB). Counting from 0000 up: 0000=0, 0001=1, 0010=2, 0011=3, 0100=4, 0101=5, 0110=6, 0111=7, 1000=8, 1001=9, 1010=10, 1011=11, 1100=12, 1101=13, 1110=14, 1111=15. This is the fundamental table for converting any 4-bit binary pattern to its decimal equivalent and underlies later BCD, hex, and truth-table work.

Page 24 ('Binary Counting') shows the standard 4-bit truth-table-style counting chart: columns headed by weights 2^3=8, 2^2=4, 2^1=2, 2^0=1 (LSB), rows 0000 through 1111 each paired with their decimal equivalent 0 through 15 -- reproduced in full in the text field above.

chunks.topic: Representing Binary Quantities: Sampling, Voltage Levels, Two-State Devices
chunks.summary: Analog signals are digitized by sampling at regular intervals; a digital signal's two states (HIGH/LOW) are defined by voltage ranges rather than exact 1/0 values, and many physical two-state devices (switches, diodes, relays, transistors, photocells) can implement binary logic.
chunks.text: Analog signals can be converted to digital form by taking measurements ('samples') of the continuously varying signal at regular time intervals; the appropriate spacing between samples depends on how fast the analog signal can change (its maximum rate of change) -- sample too slowly and fast changes are missed. Air temperature is a typical analog quantity whose recorded samples become discrete integer data points once digitized. In practice, a digital signal's two states are not exact voltages but voltage RANGES: a higher range of voltages represents a valid logic 1, and a lower range represents a valid logic 0; the terms HIGH and LOW are often used instead of '1' and '0' precisely because any voltage within the defined range counts as that state. Many physical two-state devices can be used to implement binary logic, including: a light bulb (off or on), a diode (conducting or not conducting), a relay (energized or not energized), a transistor (cutoff or saturation), and a photocell (illuminated or dark). Timing diagrams (produced by oscilloscopes and logic analyzers) plot voltage against time on a horizontal scale of regular intervals starting at time zero, letting engineers see how a digital signal changes over time or compare multiple signals against each other.

chunks.summary: Digital circuits (also called logic circuits) produce and respond to predefined voltage ranges, reacting to a signal's binary level (0 or 1) rather than its exact voltage value.
chunks.text: Digital circuits -- also called logic circuits, the two terms are used interchangeably -- are circuits that produce and respond to predefined voltage ranges. The key idea is that a digital circuit responds only to an input's binary level, 0 or 1, and not to its actual instantaneous voltage; as long as a voltage falls within the defined LOW range it is treated as a 0, and as long as it falls within the defined HIGH range it is treated as a 1, regardless of small variations within that range. This is what gives digital circuits their noise immunity, discussed in section 1-3.

chunks.summary: Parallel transmission sends all bits of a binary number simultaneously on separate lines (fast, more wiring); serial transmission sends bits one at a time on a single line, per time interval (slower, less wiring).
chunks.text: Parallel transmission sends all bits of a binary number simultaneously, which requires a separate physical line for each bit; this makes it fast but wiring-intensive. Serial transmission instead sends each bit of a binary number one at a time, at some fixed time interval, over a single line; this makes it slower but requires only a single signal path. The general trade-off: parallel transmission is faster but requires more physical paths (wires/traces), while serial transmission is slower but only needs a single path -- which is why serial links (e.g., UART, SPI, USB, PCIe) dominate for long-distance or pin-constrained communication while parallel buses are used for very short, high-bandwidth, low-latency internal connections (e.g., inside a chip or between a CPU and nearby memory).

chunks.summary: A circuit that retains a response to a momentary input exhibits memory; memory lets a system store binary numbers temporarily or permanently, using magnetic, optical, or electronic latching elements.
chunks.text: A circuit which retains a response to a momentary input is said to be displaying memory. Memory is important because it provides a way to store binary numbers temporarily (e.g., in registers/RAM during processing) or permanently (e.g., in ROM/flash/disk). Memory elements can be implemented with magnetic media (hard disks, magnetic tape), optical media (CDs/DVDs), or electronic latching circuits (flip-flops, SRAM cells) -- the latter being the building block for the sequential circuits (latches, flip-flops, registers, counters) covered later in the course.

chunks.topic: Digital Computers: Major Parts and Types
chunks.summary: A computer's five major parts are input, memory, control, arithmetic/logic (ALU), and output units -- control+ALU together form the CPU; computer types include microcomputers, minicomputers, mainframes, and embedded microcontrollers.
chunks.text: A computer is a system of hardware that performs arithmetic operations, manipulates data, and makes decisions, executing high-speed, high-accuracy operations based on a stored program's instructions. The major parts of a computer are: (1) the Input unit, which brings instructions and data into memory; (2) the Memory unit, which stores data and instructions; (3) the Control unit, which interprets instructions and sends the appropriate signals to other units; (4) the Arithmetic/Logic Unit (ALU), which performs arithmetic calculations and logical decisions; and (5) the Output unit, which presents information from memory to the operator or an external process. The control unit and ALU are so tightly coupled that they are often treated as a single block called the Central Processing Unit (CPU). Types of computers include: the microcomputer (most common, e.g., desktop PCs, now very powerful), the minicomputer/workstation, the mainframe, and the microcontroller -- a dedicated/embedded controller designed for one specific application, used in appliances, manufacturing processes, automotive ignition and ABS systems, and countless other embedded contexts. A cell phone illustrates several of these ideas at once: its digital subsystems are run by an embedded microcomputer system; when a picture is taken, the camera's CCD converts the brightness of each pixel spot into binary numbers stored in memory addressed by row/column, and displaying that image on the LCD is the reverse process (memory -> display); when a user speaks, the analog voice signal is converted into a string of digital numbers, and digital multiplexers/demultiplexers route the resulting signals to their proper destinations.
